summary:
## Verdict

**Critical security regression** — this change turns a fixed-origin CORS allowlist into reflect-any-origin with credentials, which lets any website read authenticated API responses in the browser.

## What went wrong

Previously `corsHeaders` only emitted `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` (and credentials) when the request `Origin` was in `ALLOWED` (`https://app.example.com`). The new code always returns:

- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <request Origin>` (or `*` when `origin` is null)
- `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`

That combination is the classic CORS misconfiguration exploit path: a malicious page at `https://evil.example` sends a credentialed `fetch`/`XHR` to the API; the browser includes cookies; the response is readable because ACAO echoes `evil.example`.

## Why the mobile rationale does not hold

CORS is enforced by browsers and webviews, not by native HTTP stacks (URLSession, OkHttp, etc.). Native clients that omit `Origin` never needed ACAO to call the API. For mobile webviews that do send an origin, the safe fix is to extend the allowlist (or match a known app-origin pattern), rather than trusting every origin.

Secondary issue on the same lines: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is invalid per the Fetch CORS spec; browsers will fail those responses, so the null-origin branch does not unlock credentialed access either.

## Recommendation

Restore an explicit allowlist (or origin pattern) for browser/webview clients. Keep credentials only when the reflected origin is on that list. Native non-browser clients need no CORS change.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The head `corsHeaders` always sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to the request origin (or `*`) together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, while base only did so for `https://app.example.com`. That is a real critical CORS credentialed-reflection regression.
